scenes.visual: A strip of skin cells gets a gap; a question mark in the gap; one cell splits in two, each with a question mark over its instructions.
scenes.tts: Scrape your knee. In about one to two weeks, new skin often covers the spot. Where did those new skin cells come from? Every cell comes from a cell that was already there. One cell splits and becomes two. Most cells carry a full set of instructions. How does each new cell get a complete set?

scenes.visual: Two chips in a loop, interphase and mitosis, with a nucleus holding four thin chromosome bars.
scenes.tts: A cell that divides goes through the cell cycle. It is the series of steps from when a cell forms until it divides. It has two main parts. Interphase is when the cell grows and copies its chromosomes. Chromosomes are the threads in the nucleus that carry the cell's instructions. During interphase the cell is busy, not resting. Mitosis is when the cell divides into two new cells.

scenes.visual: A model cell with four chromosomes. Each is copied into two joined bars. The counter stays at four.
scenes.tts: Picture a model cell with four chromosomes. In interphase, each chromosome is copied. A copied chromosome is still one chromosome. It is made of two identical copies joined together. So the cell still has four chromosomes. Each one now has two copies.
scenes.narration: Picture a model cell with four chromosomes. In interphase, each chromosome is copied. A copied chromosome is still one chromosome. It is made of two identical copies joined together. So the cell still has four chromosomes. Each one now has two copies.

scenes.visual: Stage tracker; chromosomes thicken (prophase), then line up in a column across the middle (metaphase).
scenes.tts: Now mitosis begins. It has four stages, and they always come in the same order. In prophase, the chromosomes coil up and get thick enough to see. In metaphase, the chromosomes line up in a row across the middle of the cell.
scenes.narration: Now mitosis begins. It has four stages, and they always come in the same order. In prophase, the chromosomes coil up and get thick enough to see. In metaphase, the chromosomes line up in a row across the middle of the cell.

scenes.visual: Copies pulled to opposite ends with thin fibers; two nuclei form and the cell pinches into two daughter cells; parent cell outlined.
scenes.tts: In anaphase, the two copies of each chromosome are pulled to opposite ends. Thin fibers in the cell do the pulling. In telophase, two new nuclei form, and the cell pinches into two. Each new cell is called a daughter cell. The cell that divided is the parent cell.
scenes.narration: In anaphase, the two copies of each chromosome are pulled to opposite ends. Thin fibers in the cell do the pulling. In telophase, two new nuclei form, and the cell pinches into two. Each new cell is called a daughter cell. The cell that divided is the parent cell.

scenes.visual: Two daughter cells, banners copy first then share, counters four each; skipping the copy leaves two each; restored to four.
scenes.tts: So how does each daughter cell get a complete set? Copying comes first. Then one copy of each chromosome goes to each new cell. Each daughter cell ends up with four chromosomes, the same as the parent cell. Skip the copying, and each daughter cell would get only two. Copy first, then share, and the instructions are not mixed up or lost.
